entries.subject: The axioms the switch-level device model rests on
entries.claim: the inclusive threshold (D3) is load-bearing: strict thresholds break every gate
entries.note: The row counts were derived by hand and written into the registration before the run. They were right. On this integer domain a strict n(t) is an inclusive n(t+1), and a device that can never conduct is indistinguishable from an absent one, so the mutation is a transformation of the device list rather than a patch to the solver.

entries.subject: The axioms the switch-level device model rests on
entries.claim: the fixed point is not unique, and an all-X start is indistinguishable from all-Z
entries.note: FAILED on its premise, not its answer. It asked which seeds of the self-inverter are self-consistent, taking for granted that every seed resolves to something. Two of three do not: seeded at a level the network runs -1 -> +1 -> -1 forever and solve() throws. That falsified N7, which claimed resolution cannot oscillate, full stop -- true only from the all-Z start, where a node on a gate CYCLE never gets a determined gate and so lands on X and stays. Nodes elsewhere firm up in gate-dependency order and may pass THROUGH X: an earlier wording of the correction said they reach X on the first pass and stay, which is false, and 481 passing checks did not notice because none of them looked at an intermediate pass. One does now. N7 was reworded to say so. The second half of X2 held exactly: 0 of 27 rows differ, because conducts() maps Z and X alike to unknown.

entries.subject: The carry cell and the six-trit adder, built out of switches
entries.claim: the assembled six-trit ripple adder is T.add, exhaustively, including the overflow trit
entries.note: The carry-out was part of the claim on purpose. Without it the circuit is a mod-729 unit rather than an adder, and a sweep that ignored it would pass on a circuit that silently discards overflow.

entries.subject: The carry cell and the six-trit adder, built out of switches
entries.claim: every pair settles in exactly seven passes, never six, whatever the carry does
entries.note: Derived before the run rather than probed: reachability is transitive closure, so a fully determined chain of switches resolves in ONE pass however long it is, and staging happens only where a gate is still unknown. Cell 0 resolves on pass 1, cell i on pass i+1, and pass 7 observes nothing changed. Ripple delay is invisible to a model with no delays in it -- the single cost a ripple adder is famous for is the one this model cannot show. Five hand-picked pairs had been checked during design; 531,441 is what made it a result.

entries.subject: The carry cell and the six-trit adder, built out of switches
entries.claim: sharing identical leaf selectors does not break the circuit
entries.note: Registered as the most likely of the five to fail. A shared leaf ties two mid-level selectors to one node, so the shared circuit contains conducting paths BETWEEN mid nodes that the tree structure did not have -- identical tables do not in general imply identical circuits, and a pass network is where that distinction bites. Here they did.

entries.subject: The carry cell and the six-trit adder, built out of switches
entries.claim: and sharing does not change the settling depth

entries.subject: The carry cell and the six-trit adder, built out of switches
entries.claim: the cost reversal against W3 is structural, not an artefact of six trits against ten bits
entries.note: W3 measured 0.80 for MIN and predicted it should not be believed. Both numbers are real and the currency did not change: MIN is positionwise, so six wide slices beat ten narrow ones, while an adder is a table and a selector tree over three inputs is 3^3 wide in ternary against 2^3 in binary. The per-digit saving is spent on tree width. The binary adder compared against was itself checked exhaustively at five bits, because a cost comparison against a circuit that does not work is not a comparison.

entries.subject: The two limits every switch count in this repository was quoted under
entries.claim: the free mid rail is load-bearing for exactly one published result, and it is the one that favoured ternary
entries.note: T5 says the generator cannot be built inside the model at all: a divider between vss and vdd is two rails reaching one node, which is contention. So this break-even is a charge from outside the vocabulary rather than a circuit that could be drawn here. What can be said exactly is how dear it would have to be, and twelve switches is not dear.

entries.subject: The two limits every switch count in this repository was quoted under
entries.claim: buffering cannot take ternary pass depth below 4, and binary gets 3 for free
entries.note: FAILED on its conclusion, not its numbers. The buffered floors are exactly as registered: 6 -> 4 -> 4 ternary and 3 -> 2 -> 2 binary. What failed is the clause that followed -- that 4 is the best depth ternary can buy AT ANY PRICE. Nothing measured quantified over designs; it quantified over where buffers go inside one family of selector trees. Decode the select instead of gating on it: a four-switch detector pulls to vss for LOW and HIGH and passes vmid for MID, paid once per select signal rather than once per selector, and then every selector arm is a single device including the middle one. The decoded adder cell reaches depth 3 -- equal to binary unrestored -- at 90 switches against 104, so it is shallower AND cheaper than the design the floors were measured on. Third time a clause in this repository outran its measurement; P3 and X2 were the others. Kept as FAILED, and the refutation is checked in test/test-midrail.js.

entries.subject: The decoded-selector adder â€” the circuit that failed Z2, at full width
entries.claim: the decoded six-trit ripple is T.add, exhaustively, including the overflow trit
entries.note: At risk in a way the selector tree was not: the carry feeds a DETECTOR as well as three raw arms, so cell i depends on cell i-1 through two paths that have to agree. They do. test-decoded.js also checks the two adders against EACH OTHER rather than both against T.add -- different primitives, same function on every sampled pair. The first sweep skipped the correctness check for any pair that did not settle inside the predicted budget, so this result was conditional on that bucket being empty. It is measured now: zero pairs need more than thirteen passes, and every one of the 531,441 was compared.

entries.subject: The decoded-selector adder â€” the circuit that failed Z2, at full width
entries.claim: 540 switches, and 360 with leaves shared

measured.decomposition: 18 detectors x 4, plus 12 trees x 13 selectors x 3

entries.subject: The decoded-selector adder â€” the circuit that failed Z2, at full width
entries.claim: read depth 3 for the whole ripple, not just one cell
entries.note: Half the selector tree, and equal to the binary adder unrestored. The chain resets at every gate and a carry is read as a gate, which is why six cells are no deeper than one.

entries.subject: The decoded-selector adder â€” the circuit that failed Z2, at full width
entries.claim: exactly 13 passes for every operand pair, still independent of the data
entries.note: FAILED on universality, not on arithmetic. Thirteen is correct as the WORST case, which is what the derivation actually bounded; the range is 9 to 13 and it DEPENDS ON THE OPERANDS. First circuit in the repository whose settling time is arithmetic rather than structural, and it scoped Y2 and Z5. Their independence-of-data result is a property of gating every arm on the RAW select, which makes all conduction known at one instant so nothing can settle early. Decoding splits the gating across two dependency levels: with the carry-in LOW the LOW arm already conducts while the MID arm gate is still unknown, so if both arms lead to the same rail the node is determined a pass early, by N3. Six of the carry table nine leaves have their LOW and MID cells equal; none of the sum table do. The three outcomes were separated on a second run: 279,936 settle in fewer than thirteen, 251,505 in exactly thirteen, and 0 in more. So 128 of every 243 settle early, and thirteen is a genuine ceiling rather than merely the predicted number. The count is no longer unexplained: the F set derives it exactly. The six agreeing carry leaves enable the saving, and the sum tree never being early is what decides which positions can use it.

entries.subject: The decoded-selector adder â€” the circuit that failed Z2, at full width
entries.claim: it narrows the gap without closing it, and taps the mid rail less
entries.note: The ratio half held exactly: 1.93 and 1.64, never below 1.36 at any width from one trit to six, and 3.21x per digit against a log2(3) break-even of 1.585. The mid-rail half was BACKWARDS. The decoded design taps vmid 186 times against 168 -- one more per detector, eighteen of them -- because each detector reaches vmid through its own series pair. So the design that wins on switch count does it partly by leaning harder on the rail Z1 established that nobody is charging for. Kept as FAILED on the X2 precedent: a prediction with a refuted half is not trimmed to the half that survived.

entries.subject: Where 128/243 comes from â€” the decoded adderâ€™s pass count, derived
entries.claim: the rule is exact pair by pair, not merely in aggregate
entries.note: Reproducing a total is much weaker than reproducing it term by term, so this was registered in the strong form. Zero disagreements against the actual solver over 597,861 pairs across five widths, every one of them exhaustive. The distribution sums to 531,441. Scoped to carry-in 0 after the fact: every sweep fixed it, and the exclusion of the bottom position is a property of that choice rather than of the circuit. Caught by asking what the sweep actually visited, which is T-CLAIM-NARROWED-BY-A-DESIGN checking itself.

measured.rule: at carry-in 0: passes = (2n+1) - #{ i in 1..n-2 : c_i != 0 and carry(s_i + c_i) == carry(s_i) }
measured.scope: carry-in 0 throughout; with a non-zero carry-in the bottom position can save as well (six of its nine digit-pairs qualify) and the walk is a different one

entries.subject: Where 128/243 comes from â€” the decoded adderâ€™s pass count, derived
entries.claim: the sum tree can never settle early, and that asymmetry is the whole result
entries.note: Early settling needs the arm conducting on the raw select and the arm still waiting on the MID detector to lead to the same rail. For the carry tree that is carry(s+c) == carry(s), true for 12 of 18, because the carry function is flat over stretches. For the sum tree it is lowTrit(s+c) == lowTrit(s), true for none of them, because adding one always moves a low trit. So only the carry tree is ever early; the top position SUM is always the last node to move; and a saving at the top position is therefore invisible. That is exactly why the earlier naive count over-predicted by one, always in the same direction.

entries.note: The matrix is derived from the adder own tables inside the check rather than written down, and comes out as nine ways from the middle carry state and three from each end. The 3^5 in the denominator is four constrained positions plus one free top digit.

entries.note: Checked against the actual circuit exhaustively at all five widths. A rule fitted to six trits rather than derived would come apart here. It does not.

entries.subject: Whether 251,505 appearing twice, from unrelated constructions, is anything
entries.claim: the correspondence dies at the first other parameter, and not narrowly
entries.note: Decisive in the bluntest available way. At width 1 the monoid acts on three points, so the entire space of functions there is 3^3 = 27 and every monoid at that width, whatever its vocabulary, is at most that. Both vocabularies do reach 27 -- at a single position the positionwise maps already give every unary function. The three-trit adder has 729 operand pairs of which 621 settle late. The monoid universe is smaller than the number it would have to match, so the failure is not a wrong value but no room for one.

entries.subject: Whether 251,505 appearing twice, from unrelated constructions, is anything
entries.claim: and the two families grow at incompatible rates, so they were never one sequence
entries.note: The recurrence was derived by hand from the transfer matrix characteristic polynomial before the run and reproduces every count to width 12. Its dominant root is irrational, so the adder family multiplies by about 7.37 per step; the monoid multiplies by about 9,315 across the only span where both are computable. Across eleven adder counts and every monoid reach in the manifest, exactly one value coincides -- the one already known.

entries.subject: Whether 251,505 appearing twice, from unrelated constructions, is anything
entries.claim: the collision is where two exponent sequences cross, once, not a pattern
entries.note: They differ at the first width and agree at the second. No formula is claimed for how the monoid ceiling grows -- two data points do not determine one, and the question did not need it.

entries.subject: Whether 251,505 appearing twice, from unrelated constructions, is anything
entries.claim: and collisions of this size are rare here, which is why one looked like something
entries.note: The instrument produced a false verdict first, and this is the fourth time that has happened here. The registration said prediction sets THAT MEASURE DIFFERENT THINGS and the first loop dropped the clause, counting 279,936 as colliding with itself because two sets record the same adder count, and 4,489 likewise because two sets share a sampling stride. Corrected by classifying each set by which library its tool imports -- derived, not hardcoded -- and requiring a collision to cross that line. The disambiguation rule was chosen after the first run, which is a degree of freedom worth declaring; it implements a clause that was in the registration beforehand, and the two excluded values are restatements of one quantity under any reading. Then a second correction, and a better one. Recording this very result put 279,936 and 4,489 into the manifest again -- as the values G4 had just EXCLUDED -- and on the next run they crossed the halves and G4 failed. The measurement had become part of the corpus it measures. A census cannot count the set that is the census; the tool and the test now drop it by matching the censusing tool name rather than an id.

entries.subject: Whether this model can carry a machine, and what charge retention would cost
entries.claim: the solver is linear in devices times passes, not superlinear as the design documents assert
entries.note: FAILED on both registered criteria, and the direction of the failure is the useful part. The exponent came in BELOW 1.0 both times - sublinear, better than predicted - because fixed per-solve overhead dominates the smallest networks and the derivation had no term for it. Above 512 devices, where overhead washes out, the spread is 1.64x and the exponent 1.088: both inside the registered band. Worse, the spread criterion was not reproducible - 3.72 on one run and 2.89 on the next, either side of the line it had been given. A criterion whose verdict depends on run-to-run noise is a defect in the prediction. The claim being tested is nonetheless settled: the solver is not superlinear, and the two documents saying so were corrected. The registration also mis-cited one of those documents as design/04-device-model.md, which is design/04-storage.md; the claim lives in design/10-integration.md, design/11-open.md and two doctree pillars, all four now corrected. CRITERION AUDIT, AFTER THE FACT: H1(a) is the first recorded bite of T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE and is confirmed NOT DISCRIMINATING. THE POINT WORTH RECORDING IS THAT H1 IS NOT AMONG THE SEVEN FAILURES THAT REST ENTIRELY ON A NON-EVIDENCE CRITERION, because H1(b) ALSO failed and is discriminating: the exponent came in at 0.917 and 0.931 against a band of [1.0, 1.2], with a run-to-run spread of 0.014, some five standard deviations from the nearest edge. So this prediction's FAILED is carried by a leg the null could not have produced, whatever happened to the spread leg beside it. See F-A-LINE-THE-NULL-CLEARS-IS-NOT-EVIDENCE.

entries.subject: Whether this model can carry a machine, and what charge retention would cost
entries.claim: so the machine is simulatable, and what is lost is sweeping it
entries.note: The registered output was the crossover, and it is the sharpest thing this set produced: a full 531,441-pair sweep fits inside an hour only up to about 4,800 devices. The six-trit adder is 624 and sits comfortably inside. The machine is ~50,000 and does not. So the machine can be RUN and cannot be SWEPT, which makes it the first subject in this repository that sits outside the exhaustive discipline every other result rests on - and the exhaustibility precondition in METHOD.md stops applying to the thing the method was built to study. CRITERION AUDIT, AFTER THE FACT: H2(a) IS NOT DISCRIMINATING AND NOTHING HAD SAID SO. The leg is a DURATION LINE -- "a 50,000-device network solves in under one second" -- which is the exact class the second bite of T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE outlawed inside this very suite, and whose prescribed repair is to assert the RATIO because a ratio survives any host. The classification rests on class membership rather than on arithmetic; for scale, the margin is 14.18x against a host-load swing this corpus has itself measured at 14.35x (4,806 sweepable devices idle against 335 loaded). THE SET'S RESULT IS UNTOUCHED: the crossover is a RATIO, and the finding that the machine can be run and cannot be swept does not depend on this leg. See F-A-LINE-THE-NULL-CLEARS-IS-NOT-EVIDENCE.

entries.claim: charge retention changes nothing in the existing corpus
entries.note: Zero differences anywhere. Derived before the run and confirmed: every circuit here is solved from a cold all-Z start, and a node with no previous value is Z under either rule. The two semantics can only diverge where a node is driven on one pass and isolated on a later one, which no existing circuit does. The comparison is not vacuous - test-headroom.js shows the two solvers DO differ on a written-then-isolated node, which is the case storage needs.

entries.subject: Whether this model can carry a machine, and what charge retention would cost
entries.claim: and it makes storage nearly free, which is why the decision matters
entries.note: A single pass gate onto an isolated node writes and holds all three trits. One switch against nineteen, and the 729-word memory drops from 48,114 switches to 4,374 - eleven times, against the five the design phase estimated. Since memory is about 93% of the machine, this is the whole decision, and it costs nothing in the existing corpus by H3. The design documents ranking this change fourth by blast radius and first by leverage were right about the ordering and understated the size.

entries.note: Reading dmux before the search is what made this worth doing properly. Its middle arm is n(selMid, MID, ...), which conducts iff the detector output is at or above MID, so the CONTRACT is that the output be non-negative exactly at MID -- not the particular table that was built. Four tables satisfy it and only one had ever been considered. Nothing at one, two or three switches computes any of them.

entries.claim: six loop-breaking cells under one enable hold a tryte, exhaustively
entries.note: At risk because six feedback loops settle inside one solve, and nothing in this project had ever solved a network with more than one loop. N7 is about loops and had surfaced consequences twice that only appeared once state arrived. It did not this time.

entries.note: The 48-switch difference is six input buffers, which T5 makes mandatory at any boundary with a primary input. Enable fan-out is free in this model and is the largest thing these numbers hide.

entries.subject: A six-trit register at switch level â€” the first sequential circuit here
entries.claim: and does not leak
entries.note: With hold asserted and the write enable low, sweeping the data over the range moves the stored tryte not at all. Strides are stated in the output rather than quietly chosen.

entries.subject: A six-trit register at switch level â€” the first sequential circuit here
entries.claim: and a read in the same solve as a write sees the old value
entries.note: FAILED, cleanly and in the opposite direction. The mechanism is exact and obvious afterwards: while the write enable is asserted the feedback loop is held OPEN -- that is the whole trick that makes the write possible -- so the cell is driven straight from its input and the seeded value has nothing holding it. S0 is a TRANSPARENT LATCH, not a flip-flop, and a transparent latch is see-through by definition. So master-slave is required and the register file is double what design/05 budgeted. design/11 had already listed this as one of five outcomes that would falsify the plan, which is the design phase working: the consequence was named before the measurement, so it could not be argued with afterwards.

entries.subject: The master-slave register J4 established was required, and the discipline it needs
entries.claim: and asserting both phases at once breaks it, in the specific way predicted
entries.note: With both phases high the structure degenerates to precisely the transparent latch J4 measured. So the non-overlap discipline is load-bearing rather than conventional, and the failure it exists to prevent was produced deliberately rather than assumed. Registering the failure mode alongside the success is the point: a structure that only works under a discipline should be shown breaking when the discipline is dropped, or the discipline reads as superstition.

entries.note: The sum being right is the lesser half. The register is read by the adder while the adder is computing the register next value, and on none of the 6,561 steps did it stop reading the OLD accumulator. That is K1 property under load, and the whole reason the J4 failure mattered.

entries.subject: An accumulator â€” the first circuit here that computes and remembers
entries.claim: and costs 672 switches
entries.note: No buffer between adder and register because the sum is already rail-driven, which is the one place T5 does not charge. B needs none either, since it only ever gates selectors.

entries.subject: An accumulator â€” the first circuit here that computes and remembers
entries.claim: and its step cost varies with the data
entries.note: Inherited from the decoded adder, which E4 measured at 9 to 13 passes depending on its operands. So a machine built on this design has no fixed clock period -- the first consequence in this project that behaves like a property of the computation rather than of the structure.

entries.subject: An accumulator â€” the first circuit here that computes and remembers
entries.claim: and it accumulates across steps
entries.note: The first computation in this repository carried out by simulated transistors holding their own state between steps, wrapping correctly where the running total leaves the tryte range.

entries.subject: Can a stored value drive a selector SOURCE terminal? The roadmap phase-0 gate.
entries.claim: under naive seeding the two selector families split, and dmux fails on exactly the two addresses that bridge two words
entries.note: Exactly the predicted shape. tmux gates every leg on the select INPUT, known at pass one. dmux gates its middle leg on a COMPUTED detector output, unknown at pass one, and N6 makes unknown conduction possible -- so the selected word is bridged to a second word and two rails reach it. At sel=MID only one word is bridged, there is no second rail, and it reads cleanly. The mechanism was derived from the solver before the run and the measurement matched it.

entries.subject: Can a stored value drive a selector SOURCE terminal? The roadmap phase-0 gate.
entries.claim: under select-resolved seeding both families read correctly
entries.note: So a stored value CAN drive a selector source terminal. The roadmap phase-0 gate passes and I0, the read mux and the address path are all viable. This prediction FIRST reported dmux at 45 of 81 -- see T-TRANSCRIBED-TABLE. The failure was in the seed, not the circuit.

measured.cases: all 3 addresses x all 27 stored patterns

entries.subject: Can a stored value drive a selector SOURCE terminal? The roadmap phase-0 gate.
entries.claim: and reading does not disturb what is stored, at any pass, not only at the end
entries.note: Checked along the trajectory rather than at the fixed point, because a suite of 481 fixed-point checks once missed exactly this. No stored trit passed through X even transiently, and a second read from the state the first one left is still correct.

entries.subject: Can a stored value drive a selector SOURCE terminal? The roadmap phase-0 gate.
entries.claim: and a 27-way one-trit read mux costs exactly what budget.js PROPOSED
entries.note: A PROPOSED term in the budget tested against a built structure and matching exactly. The formula for the read path is no longer a guess -- though the decoder and write-enable terms still are.

entries.subject: Can a stored value drive a selector SOURCE terminal? The roadmap phase-0 gate.
entries.claim: and the decoder does NOT collapse into the read mux, so the address path does not halve
entries.note: A counting argument, and it decides 243 words. A 27-way read mux has 13 internal nodes and a write path needs 27 one-hot word selects, one per word; 13 < 27, so D0 survives in the write path no matter what D1 does. design/07 suspected the two were one structure seen from both ends. They share 2.3%, not half. 243 words stays out of the sweep budget and the target machine is 81. The 2.3% figure is against the 525-switch address path as budgeted at the time of the run; the read path then moved to tmux (see B1a), so the tool re-run today reports the same 12 shared switches as 2.0% of a 603-switch path. The share changed because the basis did, not the sharing.

entries.subject: A 27-word addressed memory, built â€” and three errors in the budget formula
entries.claim: the address-path formula is wrong three ways, and net too high
entries.note: All three errors confirmed and the derived total hit within rounding. (a) the decoder term charged one 3-way selector per output LINE where a node makes three, (b) it charged a bare routing tree, which C2 shows is not a decoder, so each node needs 4 pull-downs on top of 3 route-in legs -- and "not MID" costs two of them because it is two thresholds, (c) the write term charged 6xW for a per-cell write switch that J2's 11-switch cell already contains. Plus two omissions: the complement plane and the T5 data buffers. The overcounts win, so the target machine got CHEAPER: 81 words under M1 moves 3,916 to 3,562.

entries.subject: A 27-word addressed memory, built â€” and three errors in the budget formula
entries.claim: a bare routing tree is not a decoder, and the failure is silent
entries.note: The defect was produced, not asserted. With route-in legs only, an unselected select line is Z; a Z on a write-enable gate is unknown conduction, which by N6 poisons the cell it gates. Not one write landed and 104 words were corrupted across four attempts. With pull-downs added, 4 of 4 land and nothing else moves.

measured.pulldown_cost: 4 switches per node, 52 of the decoder's 105

entries.subject: A 27-word addressed memory, built â€” and three errors in the budget formula
entries.claim: a write lands in one word and nowhere else, at every pass of the solve
entries.note: Checked along the path, not only at the fixed point, because that distinction has cost this project twice. Nothing is disturbed at any intermediate pass either. Holds under CONE-RESOLVED seeding. Under state-only seeding the array does not start at all -- 26 of 27 words corrupt on every write (T-COMPUTED-CONTROL-UNKNOWN-AT-PASS-ONE). That precondition was discovered during the run and not registered, unlike B1a/B1b which split their seeding regimes in advance; the seeder was changed mid-run to supply it.

entries.subject: A 27-word addressed memory, built â€” and three errors in the budget formula
entries.claim: and it reads back through the address path
entries.note: The first round trip through an address in this project: write word k, drop the write enable, read word k back through the tmux tree. 108 of 108. Holds under CONE-RESOLVED seeding. Under state-only seeding the array does not start at all -- 26 of 27 words corrupt on every write (T-COMPUTED-CONTROL-UNKNOWN-AT-PASS-ONE). That precondition was discovered during the run and not registered, unlike B1a/B1b which split their seeding regimes in advance; the seeder was changed mid-run to supply it.

entries.subject: A 27-word addressed memory, built â€” and three errors in the budget formula
entries.claim: and every state node is seeded, by construction
entries.note: The roadmap said a seed-completeness check should exist BEFORE the array rather than after it. This is the array, and it does. A deliberately withheld seed stays at Z and is detectable rather than absorbed.

entries.subject: Interconnect: I0 against I2, and a crossover on the axis nobody was watching
entries.claim: the crossover is in destinations, not sources, and two registered expectations are wrong
entries.note: I0 wins in exactly one corner of the surface -- one destination, three sources -- and loses everywhere else. design/06 said "I0 is the one this project is set up to win with" and the roadmap registered "I0 wins at this scale and loses badly by eight sources". Both wrong, and wrong about the AXIS: I0 grows as destinations x sources, I2 as sources alone, so the destination count decides it and the source count barely matters. Node counts were built rather than derived, which mattered: the obvious formula is wrong at S=4, the headline case.

measured.formula_that_would_have_been_wrong: ceil((S-1)/2) gives 2 for S=4; the built tree is 3 nodes

entries.subject: Interconnect: I0 against I2, and a crossover on the axis nobody was watching
entries.claim: I0 cold-starts with register sources, and a computed source inherits I2's precondition
entries.note: The first half held: I0 with register sources routes correctly under state-only seeding, because its selects are address INPUTS known at pass one. The SECOND half -- registered explicitly as the boundary, to avoid claiming too much for the topology -- is false, and its falsity is the more useful result. A computed DATA source is still rail-driven through whatever produced it, so it resolves rather than poisoning. What bites is an unresolved CONTROL node, which is unknown at pass one and gates rather than feeds. So the distinction is not computed-versus-seeded, it is CONTROL versus DATA, and T-COMPUTED-CONTROL-UNKNOWN-AT-PASS-ONE is named correctly after all. Registering the boundary is what made this measurable; predicting it correctly would have taught less.

entries.subject: Interconnect: I0 against I2, and a crossover on the axis nobody was watching
entries.claim: and I2 has two failure modes I0 cannot have
entries.note: Produced rather than asserted. And the two-enable result carries something nobody predicted: the bus goes X only on the trits where the two sources DISAGREE. 5 and -5 are trit-wise negatives, so they differ on three positions and agree (at zero) on the other three -- and the bus is X on exactly those three. A double-enable fault is therefore INVISIBLE whenever the contending sources happen to hold the same value. N4 does not say "contention is detected"; it says contention is X, and X only appears where there was something to disagree about. One correction to this audit's own first phrasing: it said "I0 has no shared node to contend for", which is false -- a tmux output IS shared between its legs. The difference is not whether a node is shared but how exclusion is guaranteed: I0 gates every leg on one select trit, so exclusion is structural; I2 needs S separate enables to be one-hot, which is an invariant something has to maintain. The comfortable phrasing was the wrong one.

exclusion.I0: structural -- every leg gated by the SAME select trit, and one trit cannot be LOW and HIGH at once
exclusion.I2: an invariant -- S separate enables must be one-hot, and something must uphold that every step

entries.subject: Interconnect: I0 against I2, and a crossover on the axis nobody was watching
entries.claim: and the decision does not belong to this phase
entries.note: SCOPE COMMITMENT, NOT A FALSIFIABLE CLAIM ABOUT THE CIRCUIT. Recorded as HELD because the phase did what it registered it would do, but flagged so it does not become a template for padding sets with unfalsifiable process entries. It is the only prediction in twenty-one sets that is about the PHASE rather than the SUBJECT. I2 is 3.8x cheaper and needs a second control cone solved and seeded every step. Whether that is affordable is a question about how a step works, and design/09 is unbuilt -- so forcing the pick here would be deciding a sequencing question inside a wiring phase. Registered in advance that deferring is the expected outcome, so that it reads as a result rather than an omission. One bound the ledger needs: its I0 row says "no cold-start precondition -- selects are inputs", which is true of the RIG and not of the machine. In the assembled machine I0 selects come from instruction DECODE, which is a computed control node, so I0 inherits a control cone there too. The real comparison is therefore ONE cone (decode, already required by any design) against TWO (decode plus bus enables) -- which sharpens the deferral rather than weakening it.

I2.precondition: a second control cone, solved and seeded every step
I2.failure_modes: X on double-enable, Z on no-enable

entries.subject: Which self-referencing ternary maps mix at all? A hashing question, answered by exhaustion at 729 states
entries.claim: a non-bijective f bleeds state and a permutation does not
entries.note: Exact. So the structural rule holds and is now measured rather than asserted: an iterated hash of this shape must use a PERMUTATION, and its compression must come from TRUNCATION at the end. A non-bijective f throws away a third of the space on the first call.

entries.subject: Which self-referencing ternary maps mix at all? A hashing question, answered by exhaustion at 729 states
entries.claim: any positionwise f has period at most 6, at every width
entries.argument: A trit permutation has order 1, 2 or 3. Applying one per position, f^m is the identity exactly when every position's is, so the order is an lcm drawn from {1,2,3} and is at most 6 — at ANY width, not just the one swept.
entries.note: The whole positionwise family is dead for this purpose, provably rather than statistically. A trit permutation has order 1, 2 or 3; applying one per position, f^m is the identity exactly when every position is, so the order is an lcm drawn from {1,2,3}. A state of ANY width returns to itself within six calls. This is strictly stronger than Q4's 27^w ceiling, because a ceiling still permits a large orbit and a period of six does not.

measured.widths: holds at any width by the lcm argument

entries.subject: Which self-referencing ternary maps mix at all? A hashing question, answered by exhaustion at 729 states
entries.claim: cross-trit coupling breaks the period bound and rotate(s + sbox(s)) resembles a random permutation
entries.note: Wrong, and wrong twice over. First the sub-claim that s + sbox(s) is not in general a permutation held, but for a reason worth more than the claim: it is injective exactly when the s-box is an ORTHOMORPHISM (see F-ORTHOMORPHISM-GATE). Second, and the actual failure: with a correct orthomorphic s-box, rotate(s + sbox(s)) still lands at 130 cycles against a baseline of 6.6. It does not resemble a random permutation at all. The reason the prediction missed is that a positionwise 3-cycle IS addition of a constant, so s + sbox(s) stays AFFINE, and affine maps over this ring have tiny order. Fixing the s-box fixes injectivity and does nothing whatsoever for mixing. Carry alone is not enough; the addend must be nonlinear in s.

first_run_registered_candidate.note: the registered candidate's actual first result, before the s-box was corrected

entries.subject: Which self-referencing ternary maps mix at all? A hashing question, answered by exhaustion at 729 states
entries.claim: truncated collisions separate a mixing f from a positionwise one
entries.note: All three land at 0.96x, indistinguishable from each other and near-ideal -- including the positionwise map that D2 proves repeats every six calls. The prediction missed because truncating ANY permutation to three trits yields exactly 27 buckets of 27, which is perfectly uniform by construction. So uniformity is what a permutation gives away for free, and a collision count CANNOT distinguish a good hash from a relabelling. This failure is worth more than the prediction would have been: it disqualifies the most obvious test anyone would reach for. CRITERION AUDIT, AFTER THE FACT: THE CRITERION COULD NOT HAVE GONE THE OTHER WAY, and here that IS the finding rather than a defect in it. Truncating ANY permutation to three trits gives exactly 27 buckets of 27, so P(the ideal outcome | any permutation-based candidate) = 1 and all three candidates were always going to land at 0.96x, including the positionwise map D2 proves repeats every six calls. This is the one entry in this audit where "the criterion was not evidence" and "the failure was valuable" are the same sentence: the note below already draws the right conclusion, and it produced AN1. The outcome stands as recorded. See F-A-LINE-THE-NULL-CLEARS-IS-NOT-EVIDENCE.

entries.subject: Reversible universality: ternary reaches it at two operands, binary provably cannot
entries.claim: the Schreier-Sims instrument reproduces four known group orders exactly, in BigInt
entries.note: Four of five on the first run, and the fifth was the TEST CASE rather than the tool: it paired a 3-cycle with a 25-CYCLE, which between them move only 25 of the 27 points, and the tool correctly returned 25!/2 -- the right answer to the question actually asked. Scored WRONG against an expectation of 27!/2. A test case that does not generate what its name says is an instrument-false-verdict aimed at the instrument instead of at itself. Both cases are now kept, the 27-point one and the 25-point one, with their correct expectations.

measured.cross_check: the M3 group enumerated by brute force (151,632 elements) matches the chain exactly

entries.subject: Reversible universality: ternary reaches it at two operands, binary provably cannot
entries.claim: binary has no non-affine two-bit reversible gate and ternary has 362,448
entries.argument: The reversible 2-bit gates number 4! = 24 and |AGL(2,2)| = 24, so every one of them is affine. Affine composes to affine, so no 2-bit set reaches the symmetric group at any width. Counting, not sampling.
entries.note: Exact, no sampling. Reversible 2-bit gates are 4! = 24 and |AGL(2,2)| = 6 x 4 = 24, so every one of them is affine. Reversible 2-trit gates are 9! = 362,880 and |AGL(2,3)| = 48 x 9 = 432. Since affine maps compose to affine, an all-affine gate set generates a subgroup of AGL however it is wired -- so binary two-bit gate sets cannot reach the symmetric group at ANY width, which is why binary reversible computation needs a three-bit gate.

measured.closure_verified_by: membership, x -> Ax + b, on every element of the generated group

entries.subject: Reversible universality: ternary reaches it at two operands, binary provably cannot
entries.claim: a named width-two ternary gate set generates exactly A_27, as its parity forces
entries.argument: INC is nine disjoint 3-cycles and each C1INC is three; a 3-cycle is even, so the generated group lies inside the alternating group. S_27 was excluded by parity before the run rather than found absent by it.
entries.note: Predicted from parity rather than left to chance: INC is nine disjoint 3-cycles and each C1INC is three, a 3-cycle is even, so the group lies inside the alternating group and S_27 was forbidden before the run. It came out exactly A_27. C1INC is non-affine because the indicator of t == 1 is quadratic over GF(3). The family half was registered separately so one gate would not be read as the family, and 20 of 20 cleared the bar.

measured.family_sample: 20 of 20 random non-affine 2-trit gates reach at least A_27, against a predicted 15 of 20

entries.subject: Reversible universality: ternary reaches it at two operands, binary provably cannot
entries.claim: the same wiring with an affine gate stays inside AGL(3,3)
entries.note: One gate changed from non-affine to affine -- same widths, same wiring, same four generators -- and universality disappears by twenty-three orders of magnitude. Checked by MEMBERSHIP and not by an order bound: all 151,632 elements were enumerated and every one is of the form x -> Ax + b. An order bound would have passed for any small group. The group is index 2 in AGL(3,3) because all four generators are even.

entries.subject: Ternary is born nonlinear at one control â€” and the whole economic margin is borrowed from the free mid rail
entries.claim: one-control single-value indicators are affine in GF(2) and never in GF(3)
entries.note: Exhaustive over one variable in both fields. This is set M's advantage traced to its root: the simplest possible conditional -- act if the control equals a specific value -- is LINEAR in binary and NONLINEAR in ternary, so binary must AND two controls together to get nonlinearity and that is why it needs a three-bit gate. Restricted to ONE control digit on purpose: the indicator of a single POINT of two binary digits is quadratic too, which is what x AND y is, so the general claim would be false.

entries.subject: Ternary is born nonlinear at one control â€” and the whole economic margin is borrowed from the free mid rail
entries.claim: the cheapest non-affine trigger is an outer state, not the middle
entries.note: The direction held and the magnitude was understated. The registration said "equals MID needs two", counting THRESHOLD COMPARISONS; the switch cost is five, because the interval test needs the whole isMid detector at four plus one select switch. So an outer trigger is five times cheaper per gate, not twice. Caveat as registered: this is the per-gate marginal cost, and E/I showed a MID detector amortises across every selector sharing a control, so in a machine it may be a wash.

entries.subject: Ternary is born nonlinear at one control â€” and the whole economic margin is borrowed from the free mid rail
entries.claim: the operand advantage does not become a switch advantage
entries.note: Both derived numbers hit exactly, and both gates verified correct exhaustively. Built in the SAME pass-network idiom with T5 obeyed on both sides -- every source rail-driven, buffers counted, no trick used on one side and withheld from the other. An earlier estimate put the binary side at ~22 by building it from NAND gates while giving the ternary side pass-transistor tricks; that strawman is recorded rather than quietly dropped. Two operands instead of three buys 1.2x, not 3x.

entries.subject: Ternary is born nonlinear at one control â€” and the whole economic margin is borrowed from the free mid rail
entries.claim: and what margin remains is borrowed entirely from the free mid rail
entries.note: The tie lands at exactly the predicted price. The device model's FIRST stated limit is that vmid is free and it calls that the largest of the four; the ternary gate takes two mid taps and the binary gate takes none. So the honest statement is not "ternary is cheaper" -- it is that ternary's advantage is STRUCTURAL and not economic, and every switch of the economic margin is borrowed from the one assumption this model flags as its biggest. A myth killed before it was built on.

entries.subject: Pricing the free mid rail: how much of this project rests on its largest assumption
entries.claim: a tap is unavoidable iff some node must carry MID, and tmux/dmux need none
entries.note: Failed two ways. (i) The selectors were predicted to need no tap; measured at 1 and 2, because the rig wires their SOURCES to the rails and the vmid source IS the tap. With abstract sources they are zero. Both readings are true of different questions -- a selector has no tap of its own and acquires one the moment it must be able to pass MID -- and the prediction did not say which it was asking. (ii) The more interesting failure: the test asks "does THIS BUILD put MID on a node", which is not the rule as registered. The rule was "must some node carry MID for the FUNCTION to compute". isMid is scored FORCED and N2 proves it is not, and the counterexample was sitting in the next section the whole time. Telling the two apart needs a search over equivalent circuits, which this test does not do.

isMid.actually: not forced -- N2 builds it with zero taps

entries.subject: Pricing the free mid rail: how much of this project rests on its largest assumption
entries.claim: the detector's mid tap is a choice, and a zero-tap variant drives every consumer identically
entries.note: Same four switches, one fewer rail. Every consumer in the repository gates a detector at threshold MID, which conducts for anything at or above it, so HIGH serves exactly as MID does. Both consumer patterns swept exhaustively. NOT tested: a decoded adder rebuilt on the variant, because dRippleAdder calls isMid internally and cannot be swapped without editing device.js -- an earlier version of this section printed "the shipped decoded adder still checks out", which exercised the ORIGINAL detector and could not have failed for the reason it claimed. Removed rather than left standing.

entries.subject: Pricing the free mid rail: how much of this project rests on its largest assumption
entries.claim: the blast radius, derived: 339 taps on the built memory, 1.15x at a price of one, and two named comparisons
entries.note: Every derived number exact. The memory multiplier is 1.15x and not the doubling that 34% on the adder would suggest, because the memory is dominated by storage cells at 18% and a read tree at zero. The decoded adder -- this repository's best circuit result -- is the MORE tap-hungry of the two families and loses to the tree adder above a price of 4.67. So the headline result survives a moderate price and not a high one.

measured.read_path_decision: does not flip -- tmux was never cheaper (960 vs 736 at 81 words); B chose it on correctness

entries.subject: Pricing the free mid rail: how much of this project rests on its largest assumption
entries.claim: and almost none of it can be engineered away
entries.note: N2 removes three taps of 339. The other 336 come from sti inverters and tBuffers whose outputs are trit-valued, and by T5 a node that must take MID must reach vmid. So the assumption cannot be designed around, only priced -- which lands "ternary is optimal for general compute" on a single physical question this model is structurally unable to answer, with a number attached to how much depends on the answer.

entries.subject: The control word, and whether instruction decode can be made to disappear
entries.claim: the control word is sufficient: an opcode-blind interpreter reproduces src/vm.js exactly
entries.note: The ground truth the rest of the set rests on. The interpreter takes the opcode only to look up its control word and then never refers to it again -- every branch is driven by a control field. If the table were missing a distinction, some program would diverge. None does. Note that this establishes SUFFICIENCY, not that the table is a good design: a table can be sufficient and still be poorly factored.

measured.compared_on: A, C, PC, output length, halted, every step

entries.subject: The control word, and whether instruction decode can be made to disappear
entries.claim: and it is eleven trits wide, injective, and too wide to fit the opcode cell
entries.note: Exactly as derived. The control word is injective, so it carries precisely the opcode information -- spread across eleven trits instead of three. And eleven does not fit in six, so the FREE version of C5 is dead: decode cannot be made to vanish by widening the opcode into the spare trits of its own cell. That is the headline, and it is a fact about this control table rather than about ternary.

entries.subject: The control word, and whether instruction decode can be made to disappear
entries.claim: and no field can be direct-encoded into a three-trit opcode
entries.note: Every registered class size matched. Registering them exactly is what made a miscount catchable, and it caught one during the derivation: an earlier version of the fit rule asked only "max class <= 9", which is correct for a ONE-trit field, and reported the three-trit ALU field as fitting on a max class of 7. The cap for width w is 3^(3-w), which for that field is 1. Caught before the registration was written rather than after.

measured.rule: a field of width w fits iff max class <= 3^(3-w)

entries.subject: The control word, and whether instruction decode can be made to disappear
entries.claim: the best jointly direct-encodable subset totals 6 trits and is jointly injective
entries.note: Wrong by exactly one trit, and wrong about injectivity. Six trits of spare capacity exist, but NO subset of fields totalling six is jointly injective on the 25 opcodes -- the fields are chunky (widths 1,1,1,1,3,1,1,2) and no combination summing to six separates every opcode. The best is five trits, with a max joint class of 3 that the one remaining trit exactly covers. So the saving is 45% of decode rather than the 55% predicted, still at zero memory cost because the spare trits were already paid for. The prediction being optimistic by one trit is the whole error.

entries.subject: Sequencing: can the step boundary live inside the circuit?
entries.claim: a driven handshake does not settle from a cold start
entries.note: The only case that is actually a handshake resolves to unknown. A request/acknowledge pair is a feedback loop of mutually COMPUTED control nodes, and this project measured what those do three times before -- unknown at pass one, and unknown conduction poisons whatever it gates. So Q3 is not available and design/09s concession stands. The first version of this section counted the two disabled cases as "settled cleanly", which would have reported Q3 as AVAILABLE on the strength of two circuits in which no handshake occurs.

measured.go_LOW: loop disabled by pull-ups; req=1 ack=-1
measured.go_MID: loop disabled by pull-ups; req=1 ack=-1

entries.subject: Sequencing: can the step boundary live inside the circuit?
entries.claim: and seeding it makes it settle to a fixed point, which is the problem
entries.note: Nothing advanced. Seed the control cone the way the memory array in C had to be seeded and the handshake resolves -- to ONE state, which a second solve does not move. So the seeding is not a workaround for the handshake: the SEEDING IS THE CLOCK, and it is external. That is the concession arriving from a different direction.

entries.subject: Sequencing: can the step boundary live inside the circuit?
entries.claim: so the concession is forced by the model, not chosen by the design
entries.note: Every state the solver returns is a genuine fixed point: re-solving from it with the same inputs returns it unchanged, across every circuit family checked. So the solver contract is that it returns a state where nothing changed, or it throws. A sequencer needs SUCCESSIVE DISTINCT states, so sequencing inside one solve would require a network that does not settle -- and not settling is an error rather than an output. Q3 is unavailable in principle here rather than merely difficult, and the concession in design/09 is a consequence of the model rather than a weakness of the design.

entries.subject: Sequencing: can the step boundary live inside the circuit?
entries.claim: but the sequencer is cheap once the step is external
entries.note: A master-slave state register plus a next-state incrementer, stepped from outside, cycles through all 27 states and returns to its start. Every part already existed. What does not exist in this model is time.

entries.subject: Erasure: what this machine destroys, and whether the price is in the object
entries.claim: information-preserving two-input operations are rare in ternary, and much rarer than in binary
entries.note: Predicted 216, 4, 18 and 198 exactly, and every one landed. The instruction map is (A,W) -> (f(A,W), W), injective exactly when each of the three columns of the table is a bijection of the three trit values -- 6^3 = 216. Binary has 2 columns and 2 permutations each, so 4 of 16. The argument was not trusted: the column criterion was checked against a direct sweep of all 531,441 pairs on a sample of tables, and agrees on every one. The gap is the point -- a randomly chosen two-input ternary operation is about 23 times less likely to be reversible than a binary one, which is the same asymmetry M1 found on the 27-point arena arriving on the 729-point one.

entries.subject: Erasure: what this machine destroys, and whether the price is in the object
entries.claim: the erasing instructions are not the ones that overwrite the accumulator
entries.note: Scored against the CLAUSE language, and the registration was ambiguous about which reading it meant -- worth stating rather than leaving for a checker to find. The header said "under the datapath state", and this tool defines that as the (accumulator, addressed word) PAIR for an address operand; under that strict reading MIN, MAX and CSUM are single fixed figures, the split is 7 fixed and 2 varying, and AB2 fails. But the clauses say "for every operand" and "depends on the operand", which only parse if the operand is a parameter rather than part of the state -- and the operand-dependence clause is not even well-formed under the pair reading. Scored on the clauses, every predicted count and every predicted membership held. The tool prints both readings side by side so neither is hidden. The load-bearing part held too: STORE erases the full 9.5098 bits and never touches the accumulator. Under the pair state it maps (A,W) to (A,A), destroying the addressed word outright -- the textbook Landauer erasure sitting in plain sight in an instruction set nobody wrote for thermodynamics, and the instruction whose name says it is SAVING something. ADD by contrast is a permutation of the entire 531,441-pair datapath, because the operand survives in memory: it is exactly the difference between ADD and K.

entries.subject: Erasure: what this machine destroys, and whether the price is in the object
entries.claim: erasure is data-dependent, exactly as settling time turned out to be in E4
entries.note: The mean 4.5033 was derived before the run as 6*(0 + 2/3 + log2 3)/3 and measured at 4.5033. CSUM was predicted never to reach the maximum and does not -- it tops out at exactly 4 bits, so a single tritwise gate cannot erase a whole tryte however hostile its operand. SHL n and SHR n erase identically at n*log2 3: one drops the high trits and one the low, and an information count cannot tell those apart, which is a real limit of this measure and not a fact about the machine.

entries.subject: Erasure: what this machine destroys, and whether the price is in the object
entries.claim: and therefore the charge is not recoverable from the program text, which is precisely the property the static count has and this does not
entries.note: FAILED, and the failure is the answer to the question the set was opened to ask. Predicted a gap for every program and a factor above two for at least one; measured a gap for two of eight and a largest factor of 1.21. Six of the eight programs charge EXACTLY their text bound, because every opcode they execute is fixed-price -- the operand-dependent instructions (MIN, MAX, CSUM, SHL, SHR) simply do not appear in them. So the static count DOES transfer, conditionally: erasure is recoverable from the program text exactly when the instruction mix is operand-independent, and this repository's programs mostly are. The tick's virtue is not lost here, it is contingent on the ISA subset in use, which is a sharper claim than either the prediction or its negation.

entries.subject: Erasure: what this machine destroys, and whether the price is in the object
entries.claim: the machine erases by convention, not by necessity: the named zero-erasure ALU generates 1,458, and admitting the reversible tables lifts it to the full symmetric group
entries.note: The first clause HELD exactly: 1,458, which is the 729 translations extended by negation, verified by sifting all 1,459 instruction maps through a chain built from two of them. The second clause FAILED, and inverts the conclusion. Admitting every one of AB1's 216 reversible tables at every operand does NOT reach the symmetric group. The orders land on a closed form, 2^W * 3^((3^W-1)/2), matching exactly at widths 1 through 5. Width 1 is the only place reversibility is free -- there the fragment IS S_3. From width 2 the fraction collapses: 324 of 362,880, then 10^-21, then 10^-100. So REVERSIBILITY DOES NOT BUY UNIVERSALITY here, and the eraser is load-bearing rather than a convention of the opcode table -- the same shape as the result that no term over {B,C,W,I} can select. Registered honestly: at width 6 the stabiliser chain had not finished after two hours on this host, so 2^6 * 3^364 is the closed form extrapolated from five exactly measured widths, NOT a measurement. "Does not finish" would be a duration claim, which is T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE and the class this project has already bitten twice; what is recorded is what was observed.

entries.subject: Can a program's cost be learned without paying it? The implied-receipt question
entries.claim: only two of the eight programs have an input-dependent step count, and they are countdown and fold
entries.note: Failed on the count, on the membership, and on its own premise. fold does NOT vary; multiply and threeway do. And the premise that five of eight execute IN was itself wrong -- ALL EIGHT do, which a broken detector had hidden. The corrected picture is sharper than the prediction and points the same way the design question cares about: reading input is universal here and cost-invariance is still the norm. FIVE OF EIGHT PROGRAMS COST EXACTLY THE SAME NUMBER OF STEPS whatever data they are handed, so their price can be published once and nobody ever needs to run them again. multiply varies only mildly, 119 to 128, because its loop is bounded by trit count rather than by operand size; the variation is in the early-exit paths, not the iteration count.

entries.subject: Can a program's cost be learned without paying it? The implied-receipt question
entries.claim: where the cost does vary it is cheaply predictable: countdown is exactly affine in its input, fitted from two runs and exact on the rest
entries.note: Exact on 200 of 200, worst error zero. Two executions price two hundred, and the ratio only improves with the size of the sweep. This is the cheapest possible refutation of an implied receipt for this program: the number can be had without doing the work, so holding the number proves nothing about work performed. Data-dependence alone establishes NOTHING -- it is necessary for an implied receipt and nowhere near sufficient.

entries.subject: Can a program's cost be learned without paying it? The implied-receipt question
entries.claim: two programs exist with identical instruction count and identical opcode histogram whose step counts differ by more than 100x, and the achievable ratio exceeds 300x
entries.note: The structural claim HELD and the number FAILED. Two programs differing in a single immediate operand -- LOADI 1 against LOADI 364 -- have the same instruction count and the same opcode histogram under both a naive linear reader and the assembler's own tokenizer, and cost 4 steps against 730. Any predictor reading only the static shape of a program returns one number for both and is wrong on one by a factor of 183. That is a counterexample rather than a failed search, and it settles the question against SYMBOL COUNTING specifically: a price computed from a program's text cannot track what running it costs. The 300x figure was optimistic for a reason worth recording -- the four-step floor of the cheap program sits in the denominator, so the ratio is 730/4 and not 364/1. Predicting a ratio without accounting for constant overhead is the same error as quoting a speedup without the serial fraction.

entries.subject: Can a program's cost be learned without paying it? The implied-receipt question
entries.claim: bits erased per executed instruction varies across the eight programs by more than 2x, and the program with the most steps is not the one with the highest erasure per step
entries.note: Failed on the number, held on the ordering. The spread is 1.68x against a predicted 2x, which is narrower than expected -- the eight programs are more alike in erasure intensity than in anything else this project has measured about them, all falling between 3.6 and 6.1 bits per instruction. But the ordering claim held: the program that runs the longest is not the one that destroys the most per step. So a currency denominated in steps and one denominated in destroyed information do rank these programs differently, just less dramatically than predicted. Choosing between them remains a decision rather than a units conversion, on a narrower margin than the prediction assumed.

entries.subject: A loop bound the program discovers, and whether that is enough for an implied receipt
entries.claim: the two-point fit that priced countdown exactly fails here, and the cost is not monotone in the input
entries.note: The same procedure that priced countdown on 200 of 200 inputs is right on 2 of 363 here -- 0.6% against 100%. And the cost is not monotone: 33 of 242 adjacent pairs run the wrong way as the input grows, which rules out any predictor built from the magnitude of the input alone. So a DISCOVERED loop bound really is a different object from a READ one, and hailstone is the first program in this repository that has one.

measured.fitted_model: steps = 2*N - 2, from N=1 (0 steps) and N=2 (2 steps)

entries.subject: A loop bound the program discovers, and whether that is enough for an implied receipt
entries.claim: a patient predictor still wins: the full cost table costs at most 729 map evaluations, re-running costs more than 3,000, and the crossover is under 100 queries
entries.note: Every one of the 729 accumulator values is resolved exactly once -- 728 evaluations, one short of the state count because the terminating value is seeded. Answering the same questions by independent re-running costs 3,777. So a predictor expecting more than SEVENTY queries should tabulate, and from the seventy-first onward every answer is free. Being genuinely discovered is therefore NOT SUFFICIENT for an implied receipt. The predictor does not have to be clever; it is allowed to be patient.

entries.subject: A loop bound the program discovers, and whether that is enough for an implied receipt
entries.claim: no single-accumulator trajectory can exceed the state space, for this map or any other, and the observed maximum sits far below the ceiling
entries.note: Demonstrated rather than asserted: every terminating trajectory was checked for a revisit and none has one, so each is a simple path through the state space and cannot exceed 729 steps. The bound is pigeonhole and belongs to the state space rather than to hailstone -- it holds for any single-accumulator map whatever. The observed maximum uses 2.61% of the available headroom, so the tabulator wins by a wide margin rather than a narrow one.

entries.subject: A loop bound the program discovers, and whether that is enough for an implied receipt
entries.claim: the cost depends only on the accumulator, so the tabulation bound is tight, and the security parameter is reachable state count rather than loop shape
entries.note: Every scratch word was poisoned before the run and all 729 answers were unchanged, so the cost really is a function of the accumulator alone and AD2's bound of 729 is tight rather than generous. The arithmetic that follows is DERIVED: each live word beyond the accumulator multiplies the tabulator's one-off cost by 729 while leaving the runner's single query untouched. Taken with AD2 this is the result of the set -- THE SECURITY PARAMETER OF AN IMPLIED RECEIPT IS REACHABLE STATE COUNT, not whether the loop bound is discovered. That is the same shape as key length, and a different design problem from the one the question started with.

entries.subject: The T/I group, and how much harmonic vocabulary a ternary space has
entries.claim: the group AB5 measured is the T/I group of musical set theory, and the same code returns 2n at every n
entries.note: AB5 measured 1,458 for the zero-erasure ALU fragment on 729 accumulator states and called it "the translations extended by negation". Run the identical construction through the identical stabiliser chain on TWELVE points and it returns 24 -- the dihedral group musical set theory has called T/I since the 1960s. So this project independently rebuilt a group that has been studied for sixty years, and AB5's conclusion is the one music theory reached from the other side: transposition and inversion preserve interval content and can never carry one set class into another. AB5 phrased the same fact as "without an eraser the named set is inert". The tryte width is not special; 1,458 is 2 x 729.

measured.generators: translation-by-1 and negation, unchanged between cases

entries.subject: The T/I group, and how much harmonic vocabulary a ternary space has
entries.claim: the number of distinct translation orbit-lengths equals the divisor count exactly, and a prime power is divisor-poor
entries.note: Exact on all four. The comparison that makes it vivid held too: 720 and 729 are ONE APART in size and have 30 divisors against 7. Every period in a Z/3^k space is a power of three, so consecutive available periods differ by a factor of exactly three and nothing sits between them. Z/27 offers periods 1, 3, 9, 27 and therefore has no analogue of the whole-tone scale, which lives at period 6, or the diminished seventh at period 4 -- not because nobody has looked, but because 6 and 4 do not divide 27. NARROWED AFTER THE FACT: this was first written up as "a place ternary is structurally worse", which is the numbers right and the noun far too big. What is measured is ONE musical affordance -- how many chords transpose onto themselves -- and it says nothing about consonance, rhythm, contour or timbre, nor about ternary used as an ADDRESSING scheme rather than a tuning. The surviving claim is that a PRIME-POWER pitch-class space is poor in transpositional symmetry. It does NOT say binary does better -- nothing measured here bears on that, and asserting it would have been the same error one layer down.

entries.subject: The T/I group, and how much harmonic vocabulary a ternary space has
entries.claim: Burnside over the T/I group reproduces published Z/12 musicology, then gives Z/27 between 2.4 and 2.6 million set classes
entries.note: The load-bearing part is the control. Four figures -- 224, 12, 29 and 50 -- are in the musicological literature and were not derived here, and the instrument reproduced all four before its ternary answers were looked at. An audit that agrees with sixty years of published counting on the case where the answer is known has earned the case where it is not. Z/27 lands at 2,493,726, near 2^27/54 because at that size the identity element dominates the Burnside average. Worth noting the nuance the prediction did not ask for: Z/27 has 61 trichord classes against Z/12's 12, so ternary space is RICHER in raw variety while AE4 shows it is far poorer in structure.

entries.subject: The T/I group, and how much harmonic vocabulary a ternary space has
entries.claim: the fraction of subsets with nontrivial transpositional symmetry is above 2% in Z/12 and below 0.001% in Z/27, a drop of more than three orders of magnitude
entries.note: Failed on one threshold and held on everything that mattered. Z/12 measures 1.81% against a predicted above-2%, so the prediction was optimistic by a fifth. The Z/27 clause held at 0.000380% against a predicted below-0.001%, and the gap held at 3.7 orders of magnitude against a predicted more-than-three: Z/12 is 4,755 times richer in transpositionally symmetric subsets. Those are the chords Western harmony leans on -- the augmented triad, the diminished seventh, the whole-tone scale -- and a prime-power space has a single unbranched chain of subgroups and almost none of them. The failure is a reminder that a threshold picked to sound decisive is a worse prediction than the ratio it was standing in for, which is the same lesson T-CRITERION-IN-THE-NOISE keeps teaching in a different costume.

entries.subject: Which musical layers favour which base, and whether any pure radix is good for music
entries.claim: a division is good at some intervals and bad at others, so "ternary tuning is bad" is false as stated
entries.note: All three clauses held: 27-EDO's fifth is 4.68x worse than 12-EDO's, its harmonic seventh 3.48x better, and its minor third better at 4.53 against 15.64. But the sweep answered a bigger question nobody asked. SUMMED OVER THE SIX JUST RATIOS, 27-EDO TOTALS 45.48 CENTS OF ERROR AGAINST 12-EDO'S 64.41, and 81-EDO totals 22.84. A ternary division of the octave is not merely defensible on consonance, it BEATS twelve. The withdrawn claim that "ternary is genuinely worse for music" was not just too broad, it was wrong in the opposite direction on the axis it never measured.

entries.subject: Which musical layers favour which base, and whether any pure radix is good for music
entries.claim: the divisor advantage AE2 found belongs to compositeness rather than to binary
entries.note: Exact on every clause. No power of two or three below 100 exceeds 7 divisors, while 60 has 12. The counts of 32 and 27 differ by exactly the predicted maximum of 2, so POWERS OF TWO ARE POOR ON THE SAME SCALE AS POWERS OF THREE. AE2 was never a binary-versus-ternary result and should never have been written up as one: 12 = 2^2 x 3 is a power of neither radix, and the advantage it has belongs to compositeness.

entries.subject: Which musical layers favour which base, and whether any pure radix is good for music
entries.claim: rhythm does not favour ternary either, and base two gets more of the common subdivisions
entries.note: Held exactly, and it refutes something said in this conversation without measuring: that rhythm favours base three. It does not, on the ordinary repertoire. Base two represents three of the six common subdivisions exactly and base three represents one, because Western notation is halves, quarters and eighths. The two neither base gets -- a sixth and a twelfth -- are exactly those with both 2 and 3 as prime factors, and base six gets all of them. Compositeness again, from a completely different direction.

entries.subject: Which musical layers favour which base, and whether any pure radix is good for music
entries.claim: the n minimising consonance error and the n maximising divisor count are both divisible by 2 and 3, so music wants both primes at every layer
entries.note: FAILED, and the failure is the useful part because it shows the layers DECOUPLE rather than agree. The n with the lowest total consonance error between 5 and 72 is 53, which is PRIME -- divisible by neither 2 nor 3 -- and 31 is close behind at 18.19. The divisor clause held (60, divisible by both) and the beaten-by-a-smaller-composite clause held for both radices. So the tidy unifying story was wrong: HARMONIC SYMMETRY AND RHYTHM WANT COMPOSITENESS, AND CONSONANCE DOES NOT CARE ABOUT IT AT ALL. Consonance is a question about how well n*log2(r) lands near an integer, which has nothing to do with how n factors, and the prime divisions that microtonalists favour are exactly the counterexample. Predicting that three layers would agree was reaching for a single sentence where the measurement supports two.

entries.subject: The second knob: state width, evaluation cost, and what an implied receipt actually rests on
entries.claim: every program here has a live control-state width of at most 2, including the interpreter, so no program is tier three
entries.note: FAILED, and the failure produced a factor the whole thread was missing. threeway measures FIVE live input words -- it classifies five values and every one changes the path -- which is above AD4's three-word threshold and refutes the prediction. But its cost spread across the entire sweep is 1.02x, from 55 steps to 56. A tabulator facing 729^6 states to learn a number that is always 55 or 56 would not tabulate; it would guess 54 and be right almost always. Meanwhile countdown has width ONE and a spread of 25.38x. SO WIDTH AND COST VARIANCE ARE INDEPENDENT, AND NEITHER IS THE SECURITY PARAMETER ALONE. The interpreter clause held and then some: interp measures 0, not the predicted 2, because the program it interprets is assembled into its own image and is identical on every run.

measured.widths: countdown 1, fold 0, hailstone 1, interp-core 0, interp 0, kleene 0, multiply 1, tgate 0, threeway 5
measured.step_counter_convention: counts the instruction about to run, so a bare HALT costs 1 -- matching the convention AC recorded, where countdown is 5N+3 and reads 8 at N=1

entries.subject: The second knob: state width, evaluation cost, and what an implied receipt actually rests on
entries.claim: a purpose-built three-input program measures a live width of exactly 3 in fewer than forty instructions, crossing AD4 threshold
entries.note: Held exactly. A nested loop over three loaded words -- outer count, inner subtrahend, starting value -- gives a live width of 3 in 28 instructions, and each of the three demonstrably moves the cost. The state space is 729^4 = 282,429,536,481, past what AD2's tabulator could afford. The point is that WIDTH IS A PROPERTY OF THE HARNESS, NOT THE MACHINE: nothing about the ternary datapath prevented this, and no existing program has it only because none of them was written to take its work as runtime input. Reported in instructions rather than cells because the prediction was in instructions and an instruction is two cells.

entries.subject: The second knob: state width, evaluation cost, and what an implied receipt actually rests on
entries.claim: one device-level solve of the six-trit adder costs more than 5,000 node-updates against 1 for a VM instruction, at 13 passes
entries.note: The magnitude clause held for the decoded family at 5,400 node-updates and failed for the tree family at 4,368; the pass clause failed outright. Two separate errors, both about importing a constant across the conditions it was measured under. First, the registration cited E4's thirteen while the first version of the tool built the TREE adder, and E4's thirteen belongs to the DECODED one -- the same design note records the tree at 7. Second, thirteen is E4's MAXIMUM over operand pairs, not its typical value: E4 measured 9 to 13 and called the data-dependence its finding, so quoting the ceiling as though it were the number was quoting a result against its own headline. Both families are above 1,000x, which is what the argument needed; only one clears 5,000.

entries.subject: The second knob: state width, evaluation cost, and what an implied receipt actually rests on
entries.claim: the device-level work factor is worth between one and two extra words of state
entries.note: Held. log(5,400)/log(729) = 1.304, so redefining a tick from one VM instruction to one device-level solve buys slightly more than one word of state for free. WORTH HAVING AND NOT SUFFICIENT ALONE, which is the honest shape of the answer: the work factor imported from WaveSeeds is a real second knob, it is already built into the switch-level machine this project spent its life on, and it moves the tabulator's bill for a 729-state arena from 729 evaluations to 3,936,600 node-updates. The state still has to be widened.

entries.subject: Building the receipt spec, and what the attack on it actually costs
entries.claim: the three-word program clears the variance bar threeway failed, with a spread above 50x
entries.note: Held by an order of magnitude: 513.8x against a predicted 50x, and 88 distinct costs across 120 runs. So the three-word program satisfies the FIRST item of AG's spec, which is the one that matters most -- threeway had five live words and a spread of 1.02x, which is a wide state no tabulator would bother indexing. Width without variance is security theatre; this has both.

entries.subject: Building the receipt spec, and what the attack on it actually costs
entries.claim: memoisation collapses: the three-word program reuses each distinct control state fewer than 1.5 times, against hailstone above 4
entries.note: FAILED on the number that mattered and produced a FOURTH factor. The hailstone clause held enormously at 10.43x -- and its 3,777 visits reproduce AD2's figure exactly, which is the cross-check that the two sets are measuring one thing. But the three-word program still reuses each state 3.20 times, not the predicted under-1.5. The reason is structural: an input sharing its subtrahend and outer count with another converges onto the same inner-loop suffix whatever its starting value, so a subtractive loop has heavy suffix convergence BY CONSTRUCTION. WIDENING THE STATE DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY DESTROY SHARING. Convergence is a property of the map, not of the state count, and a tabulator exploits convergence rather than smallness. Reuse fell 3.3x, which is real, and nowhere near enough to call the sharing dead.

entries.subject: Building the receipt spec, and what the attack on it actually costs
entries.claim: AG4 overstated: extra state multiplies only the attacker cost while a work factor multiplies both, so the ratio improves only with state
entries.note: Held exactly, and it corrects AG4. Widening the state by one word multiplies the attacker's bill by 729 and leaves the honest cost at 1,150 steps, untouched. Moving to a device-level tick multiplies BOTH by 5,400 -- the honest party pays 6,210,000 node-updates for the same run. SO THE RATIO GAINS 729x FROM STATE AND EXACTLY 1x FROM THE WORK FACTOR. AG4 called the work factor "worth slightly more than one word of state", which treats the two as one currency; on the asymmetry it is worth nothing at all. What it buys is ABSOLUTE infeasibility -- turning a cheap attack into an expensive one in wall-clock terms -- which is real, is what a KDF is for, and is a different claim. AG4 never measured the honest side, which is the only place the difference shows.

entries.subject: Building the receipt spec, and what the attack on it actually costs
entries.claim: tabulating costs more than 10^11 state-evaluations against fewer than 300 honest steps, a ratio above 10^8, identical at either tick level
entries.note: FAILED on both magnitudes and held on its structural point. The control space is (w, b, c) = 729^3 = 387,420,489, not the 10^11 predicted -- that figure was 729^4, which counts a fourth word this program does not have, since its step counter never gates a branch.
